chapters.title: Chapter 40 — The Restoration and the Sfax Call

spans.text: Eleni was at her desk by seven forty.

The brief came in at eight oh nine, time-stamped at the encrypted gateway. It was not among the four-line summaries her assistant had drafted on Friday afternoon; it had landed after the assistant had gone home for the weekend. She marked it for first reading and went back to the summaries.

On the credenza behind her desk in the Macquarie Street office stood the harbor photograph her aunt Aspasia had given her at her admission ceremony in 2014. Eleni had carried it through three offices because Aspasia would have noticed if she had not. A sponge boat at the Pothia harbor wall, black and white, three men in the bow, the year on the back in Aspasia's hand. She had stopped registering it as anything but furniture some years ago.
At eight thirty she made a cup of instant coffee at the kitchenette down the corridor, came back, and opened the brief.

Aidan Holloway, of Holloway and Pereira, Perth. Mid-tier Perth commercial; she had heard of the firm two years earlier through a discovery exchange on a charter dispute. The instructing client was the Dampier Pearl Coast Group, registered out of a Subiaco serviced office, principal place of business stated as the same Subiaco address. Eleni noted the registered-against-principal collision and set it aside. It was the kind of detail that meant either nothing or a great deal, depending on the next ten emails.

Holloway's brief ran three paragraphs. The first named the matter: a chain-of-title review on a parcel of historical oyster-bed leasehold along the Dampier Peninsula coast, extracts attached. The second named the scope. Opine on the cleanness of the chain. Recommend a disposal pathway for any encumbering 1907-era pearling claims. Advise on procedural posture under the Western Australian instruments. The third named the fee, which was generous, and the timeline, which was Friday week. The client, Holloway wrote, would prefer that the opinion not require further conferences beyond what was strictly necessary.

That was not a line a client wrote to save money. It was a line a client wrote to a lawyer it had decided in advance would be told only what it chose to tell, and asked to file before she could learn the rest. She had seen the formulation twice before. Both times the parcel had moved while the opinion was still open on her screen.

None of it was a reason to decline. She had drafted forty clean disposal opinions in the last two years, and thirty-eight had been exactly what they appeared to be. The other two had not, and she had charged for the difference, and the clients had paid it without argument, because the difference was the reason they had briefed a Sydney maritime lawyer instead of someone closer and cheaper.
She opened the registry extract.

A 1907 Greek shipping registry. Four vessels, four Greek-Australian master names, the kind of register a Lloyd's-trained clerk in Singapore would have kept and a Darwin port officer stamped. The transshipment dates ran Singapore to Darwin in the late spring of 1907 and onward to Broome and Cygnet Bay by midwinter. The vessel names were the kind a Kalymnian crew would have given its boats, three saints and one place. Eleni knew two of the saints from the calendar her aunt kept in her kitchen and one from the parish in Pothia she had stood in once at twelve.

The chain ran from the registry forward through six transfers, the last in 1989, into the consortium's predecessor holding company by 1997. No gaps. Holloway had attached the metadata from the consortium's own digital records in a clean index.

The cleanness was the part that asked to be looked at. Eleni had learned in her second year that a chain running clean across eighty years through six private transfers and an interstate border was a chain someone had cleaned. The Department of Transport had never kept pre-1950 pearling-fleet records the way a logistics company kept its 1995 paper. Gaps were what 1907 registry chains looked like. The absence of gaps meant labor had gone into the absence. She had a name for the place in any file where the documentation got too tidy to be the truth. She called it the seam.
She wrote three lines on her notepad. Then she wrote the acceptance.

It was four sentences. She confirmed the instruction and the timeline, named her standard hourly and a not-to-exceed cap consistent with Holloway's fee, and asked him to confirm the principal place of business as the Subiaco serviced office for invoicing and conflict-check purposes. The further question the collision invited she would ask on Wednesday. Today was Monday. She sent the acceptance at nine seventeen.

Annabel Wieland was at the corridor printer when Eleni came back with her second instant coffee at nine forty. Wieland was fifty-four, managing partner for four years and at the firm twenty-two before that, and she had a habit of standing at the communal printer while a red-marked draft came through. The habit gave her corridor time. She used it.
You took the Holloway brief,
spans.speaker: Wieland

spans.text: Wieland said, not looking up.
Yes.
Good.
She sorted the pages into the order she wanted.

The Dampier group's parent is in conversation with us about an in-house secondment. Not for you. For the property team. We have been positioning for it. The Holloway brief is the kind of brief we are positioning to receive more of.
I understand.
I do not need you to do anything with the brief that the brief does not need. I want you to do it, and do it well, and send Holloway a clean opinion by Friday week.
I will.
Good.
spans.speaker: Wieland

spans.text: Wieland put the stapled draft under her arm and glanced at Eleni's cup.
That is not coffee.
spans.speaker: Wieland

spans.text: She had said the same thing on perhaps a hundred mornings. She went back toward her own office. The corridor time was over.
Eleni spent the next two hours pulling the consortium's deed chain into a procedural table she could read without the consortium's framing laid over it.
The 1989 transfer was the one she stopped on first. The transferor of record was the estate of a Sydney testator named Manolis Argyros, deceased that year.

Argyros was a common surname. There had been Argyroses in Broome and Darwin and Sydney since the 1890s, and the line had branched more than once. She did not know a Manolis. She had a great-uncle in Broome whose older brother had died some time in the late 1980s, and whose name she would have to look up in the Christmas-card list her mother had kept until 2017. She did not look it up. She placed the entry under prior owner of record and moved on.
The 1997 transfer into the consortium's predecessor was clean by the same measure. The estate's executor was a Sydney barrister named Ronald Pavlou.

She stopped on that one longer. She knew the name and did not know how, the way she knew a hymn heard once at a wedding at fourteen. She made a small notation in the margin, the single character she used for entries she expected to come back to and did not expect to enjoy coming back to. She had perhaps a dozen such characters. Her father had taught her three of them across a kitchen table when she was articled, and she had built the rest herself, and she no longer knew, looking at the margin, which three were his.

She finished the table at eleven forty with the four vessel names pulled clear at the top of it, the way she pulled the load-bearing entries clear of any file. She would highlight them tonight. The yellow highlighter was at home.

The rest of the day went to her other matters: a salvage claim on a Newcastle bulk carrier, a discovery response on a charter dispute running since November, a phone conference with a client in Auckland.

Holloway's reply on the principal-against-registered query came in at three twenty. Two lines. Subiaco serviced office confirmed for invoicing. Principal place of business under review pending the consortium's restructure. Eleni gave the formulation its heading, which was answer that is not an answer.

She would have left it there if not for the time on it. Her query had gone out at nine seventeen. The reply had come back at three twenty, which was nine twenty in Perth. A genuine restructure query took a day to answer, because the answer had to be asked of someone, and that someone had to look. This answer had been ready before she sent the question, the way a thing is ready when the person holding it has been watching for the question and has decided in advance what to give back. She had no heading for that. She filed it under the nearest one, too quick, and did not like the entry, and wrote nothing back.

At three forty she went down to the ground-floor cafe for a real coffee, because Wieland had been right about the instant. Stelio, the Greek-Cypriot barista, said what he had said to her on Mondays since about 2020, that she should try the spanakopita. She said she would try it next week. He laughed, because they both knew she would not.

At four fifty Holloway sent a second email attaching two further deed scans from the consortium's 1972 transfer, which he said had been left out of the morning's bundle. The 1972 transfer was unremarkable on its face. The transferor was a Broome holding company wound up in 1971. The transferee was a Manolis Argyros, the same name the 1989 entry carried as testator. The wind-up date and the transfer date were eleven months apart. She placed the gap under anomaly to revisit. She did not pull the 1972 transfer clear of the table. She would look at it tomorrow.

At five forty she caught the train westbound to Marrickville and walked the eight blocks home, past the Greek bakery whose owner had stopped calling her koritsi mou because she had asked him to, past the council's concrete planter of rosemary no one had asked for.

In the kitchen the Pothia calendar her aunt sent every Christmas hung by the refrigerator, the saint's days in Aspasia's pencil. Aspasia's Tupperware of loukoumades stood on the counter, a paper towel under the lid to keep the syrup from sweating. Eleni made tea, ate one loukoumas standing up, and sat down with the laptop and the highlighter from the drawer with the takeaway menus.
She drew the yellow over the four vessel names in turn. It dragged on the third, where the printer's ink had not quite taken, and she went over it again. Then she looked at them.

They sat in registry order, the order the Singapore clerk would have entered them in 1907 and the order Holloway had reproduced. Three saints. One place. The pattern, though Eleni did not yet have any word for it, was already there in front of her, in the four initials at the front of the four names, in the kind of over-ordering a chain-of-title lawyer trained to find seams would notice inside a week. She did not notice it tonight. Nor did she look at the calendar by the refrigerator, open to a month with two saint's days in pencil and one Aspasia had circled, the feast of Saint Nicholas.
She closed the laptop and thought about the Pavlou name.

It was not a memory. It was a name spoken in the next room when she was eight or nine and kept in the part of her hearing a child files without system. Her father had known a Pavlou. She was reasonably sure of it. Whether it was the Ronald Pavlou on the 1997 transfer she did not know, though Sydney barristers named Pavlou were not so many that the coincidence held no interest.
She was in bed by ten forty and lay a long time awake.

She thought about her father the way she did about once a month, as the man at the kitchen table of the Kingsford house on a Saturday morning in winter, in the cardigan her mother had knitted him in 1985. The brief had brought a thing into the flat she had not yet named, and her father had been a man who knew what to do when a clean file was too clean and someone on the other end was too quick. She had never asked him what he did. She had filed the not asking.

She decided one thing before she slept. In the morning she would pull the 1972 transfer clear of the table. The Manolis Argyros on the 1989 transfer she would leave under its heading a while longer, the way she left a thing she suspected she would not enjoy moving, because a file was easier to keep at arm's length before a name in it might be one of hers.
Tuesday Eleni was at her desk by seven thirty.

She had slept badly, and on the train she listed the reasons in the order she trusted them: the second instant coffee, the loukoumas, the name on the 1997 transfer that her hearing had filed when she was eight and handed back to her in the dark without being asked. She was persuaded by none of them, and set the list aside the way she set aside a witness who had answered a question she had not put.

She cleared three other matters first: a reply to the Auckland client on a settlement point she had drafted at five past one that morning and held, because the one-in-the-morning drafts were the ones she had trained herself to hold; a note to the discovery file on the November charter dispute; a countersignature on a vessel-purchase financing the client had needed at the close of yesterday and had not chased.
At eight forty she opened the Holloway brief and read the four vessel names at the head of her table once.

Then she read them the slow way, the pass she ran on the entries a chain of title turned on. A senior associate had drilled the method into her at her first firm in 2014, a woman who had since gone in-house at a Brisbane insurer, and it had long since stopped being a method and become the only way Eleni knew to read a register. It ran on one principle. The documents a client handed a lawyer were the documents the client wanted read. The thing the client did not want read was legible to a lawyer who knew where the absences lived: gaps, coincidences, cleanness where the record had no reason to be clean, an order that ran the way a registrar would have entered it and produced a result a registrar would never have produced.
She wrote the first letter of each name at the head of her notepad, one per line, in the order the registry gave them. Four letters.
She ran the alphabetical pass first, because it was the cheapest. Rearranged by name, the initials produced nothing. She had not expected them to. She struck a line through it.

The masters-by-seniority pass took longer, because the careers had to be cross-checked. She pulled the Lloyd's listing extracts from the registry's appendix and laid the four masters out by date of first command. The senior man had taken his in 1881, on a Symi-registered boat that appeared nowhere else in the chain. The youngest had taken his in 1899. The two in the middle were eight years apart and had each held two commands before the one the registry named. Oldest to youngest, the initials formed nothing. Youngest to oldest, the same nothing. She struck the line.

Three of the four vessels had been registered at Pothia and the fourth at Symi. A registrar of the period would have entered the two ports alphabetically and the vessels under each port alphabetically. She arranged them that way and read the initials. Not a word. Not the front of a word.
She set the pen down.

Four passes. One produced a pattern. Three did not. The one that did was the order she had written down before she ran any of them, because the first thing she did with any sequence was copy it down as given. In the order the clerk had entered them, the four initials spelled a thing.

They spelled it the way a phrase spells itself to a person who heard it in a kitchen on Sunday afternoons until she was twelve. Heard and not studied. Held without system. She understood it and did not understand it, and the understanding was not a thing she could have built from the alphabet by accident.

She did not write the gloss beside it. She had been trained out of writing down what she had no evidentiary basis to write, and she had spent the years since extending the training past the file and into her own kitchen at eight years old. She read the initials one more time and then did not read them again, which was the only sign she let herself register of what the reading had cost.

It was the kind of phrase a man at the harbor wall would have said to another man at the same wall in 1907, in a register she did not own from her own use. She knew it from the part of her hearing that had filed a name when she was eight, and from a Sunday in 1998 in her grandfather Kostas's kitchen in Kingsford, when she had been eight and Kostas had read something from a small cardboard envelope at the table in the voice he kept for the things he wanted the room to hear once and not ask about.

She did not pursue the recollection. She went to the file note and typed the heading the file permitted: Registry sequence anomaly, flag for client clarification. She typed the four initials and the four passes. Only registry order yields the sequence. She did not type what the sequence was. She typed: pending verification of 1907 Lloyd's registry sequencing conventions for Greek pearling-fleet entries through Singapore transshipment. She saved the note.
The notepad page she set face down under the manila folder with the Newcastle salvage claim, where Wieland would not see it if Wieland came in for a corridor exchange.

The deeds took the rest of the morning and most of the afternoon. She built the chain out from 1907 to 1989 and added the 1972 transfer Holloway had sent through at four fifty on Monday. The Broome holding company wound up in 1971 had been registered in 1968 by a Perth firm she did not know and dissolved by a different Perth firm she also did not know. The eleven months between the wind-up of record and the 1972 transfer that followed it were still the eleven months. A company could not transfer a parcel eleven months after it had ceased to exist, and the dates said it had. She would pursue them on Wednesday, if Holloway's answer on the registered address gave her cause.

The 1989 transfer she stopped on again, briefly, the way a hand goes back to a tooth. Manolis Argyros, deceased that year. She left the entry under its heading and did not look up the great-uncle's brother. The leaving was a small act of discipline, and she registered it as one, and did not examine why it had cost a discipline at all to leave a common surname under a heading the table had built for it.

At one fifteen Wieland passed the office door and asked whether the Holloway opinion was on track for Friday week. Eleni said it was. Wieland went on down the corridor without stopping at the printer. There was no corridor time today.

At three Eleni took a forty-minute discovery call with a junior solicitor at the Auckland client's local agent, who asked questions in the order they wanted to be asked, and not one of them was the question on the back of the page under the manila folder.

At four forty-five she sent Holloway a short query asking him to confirm the registered address of the 1972 Broome holding company at the date of its wind-up. The larger question the principal-against-registered collision had invited she would put on Wednesday, separately. The under-review formulation entitled her to two. She had now sent one.
At five fifty she packed the laptop and the notepad into her bag and caught the train westbound.

At home the yellow highlighter sat on the kitchen table where she had left it on Monday night. She picked it up to put it in the drawer with the takeaway menus, because she did not need it tonight, and then set it back beside where the laptop would go, because she did, and she did not ask herself why, because it was not a question she would have answered honestly at the sink at ten to seven on a Tuesday.
She made tea and did not eat. She opened the note.

She read the four initials once on the screen and once aloud, under her breath, in registry order. The phrase was the phrase. She heard it for a moment in her grandfather's voice, then in her own, and then in no voice at all, which was the voice she preferred for a thing she did not yet know what to do with.

She ran the passes once more on paper, with the highlighter, in case the yellow surfaced something the screen had not. Nothing surfaced. Only registry order produced the pattern, and only registry order would, on any surface she ran it on, because the pattern was not in the method. It was in the names.

That was the part she sat with. The method was hers, taught and sharpened over twelve years. The pattern was not a thing a method found. It was a thing a person had built: four boats named so their first letters would carry a phrase in the order a registrar would file them, by someone who had known a Lloyd's clerk in Singapore would copy the entry down as given and a court would read past it. A method could find a seam. It took a person to sew one. Someone had sewn this in 1907 and meant it to be read by someone, and the someone it had been meant for was not a Sydney maritime lawyer in 2026, and yet here it sat on her table, and she did not like how little distance there was between those two facts.

She thought about her grandfather, with the discipline she kept for her father, which was to refuse the romance of it. Kostas had died in 2004, when she was fourteen. At the funeral at the parish in Earlwood the priest had spoken in Greek about the harbor wall at Pothia and the boat Kostas had loaded sponges onto in 1949, a boy of seventeen, with his older brother beside him. The brother had stayed at Pothia a season longer and come out later by a different ship to a different port, and the two lines had not lived in the same city again. That was the half she had understood. She had not asked for the rest, because asking was not what the family did on the wide front lawn in Kingsford that October afternoon, with the platters out and the men of her grandfather's generation in their good suits in the heat, saying to each other the things they said instead of the things they did not.
She had not written down what Kostas said at the kitchen table in 1998. She had not written it at eight, and she did not write it at thirty-six.

Then her father, at the Kingsford table in winter in 1992, in the cardigan her mother had knitted him. The note on her screen had been typed in the procedural register Yiorgos had trained her in by example, without once saying he was training her. It was not yet the kind of note he had been asked to write at the Vryonis matter in 1981, because she did not yet know what the four initials were for, or what she would do with the knowing once she could not return it to the cardboard envelope on the shelf in Kingsford.
She folded the notepad page and slid it into the back of the manila folder she had carried home in her bag. Then she added a single line to the bottom of the file note, read it, and left it.
Order is not accident. Someone built this, and built it to be found.
Eleni drove to Tempe on Saturday morning.

She had slept four hours. By six twenty she was at the kitchen table with tea and the four initials on the back of a Coles receipt; she had been copying them onto whatever surface was near her since Tuesday. She had not written the gloss in three days and did not write it now. She put the receipt in the back of her wallet.

She dressed for the unit in jeans and an old shirt of her mother's. She had been driving out four or five times a year since her mother died in 2017, and had cleared only the front quarter of the boxes, the quarter her mother had labelled in red marker: seven years of tax records, the bank statements, the parish certificates, the deeds for the Kingsford house she had sold in 2018 to settle the estate. The back half was what her father had moved in himself the week before he died in 2019.
She had not opened the back half.
The yellow highlighter was in her bag. She had not asked herself why.

The facility sat on the industrial side of the line, two streets back from the Princes Highway, the nearest one her father would drive to in 2017. She arrived at seven thirty-four, signed the log, and lifted the roller door on her unit at the back of the third corridor.

It smelled the way it smelled in May, of dust and concrete and the faint sweet of an unopened crate of olive oil Aspasia had sent her father in 2018, with the instruction not to open it until Easter. He had not opened it by the Easter of 2019. Aspasia had not asked Eleni about it in seven years. Eleni had not opened it either.
She set up the folding chair beside the box of tax records she had been clearing in February, and looked at the box, and did not open it.

She went to the back half instead, around the leather lounge her mother had kept under plastic, past the Greek-language newspapers tied by year with twine, past four boxes labelled in red marker as Pothia photo albums, one of four through four of four. Eleni had opened one of those in 2018 and had filed the other three under a heading the unit kept for her, which was come back when you can.
She came to the law books. Three boxes, labelled in her father's hand: Yiorgos law one of three, two of three, three of three.

The first held the Halsbury's volumes from the eighties, navy spines, leather corners cracked, the small adhesive flags still tagging the sections he had used in practice; under them the conveyancing manuals he had bought as an articled clerk in 1973; under those the bound NSW Reports for 1979, 1980, 1981, 1982. The second held criminal procedure texts, property law treatises from the nineties, three loose-leaf folders of CPD materials. She resealed both.

The top layer of the third was maritime law texts she had not known he kept. Under them sat a flat cardboard box, the kind a ream of printer's paper came in, taped shut with browned masking tape and labelled on the lid in the small block capitals he used for things he did not want lost.
V v A 1981, do not destroy.

She read it twice, because she had been trained to read a load-bearing line twice before filing it. She set the box on the leather lounge beside her bag and sat down with her hands on her knees and did not lift the lid. She had come to pull tax records. Her father had taped this one box shut among three boxes of books and given it an instruction he had given no other box.
Behind the bound Reports, where the box had sat, there was a brown parcel wrapped in paper and tied with twine. She lifted it out and did not unwrap it.

She put the box and the parcel in the boot of the car, came back and repacked the third box in the order she had emptied it, and resealed it with tape from the roll on the shelf. The tax records could wait for Sunday. She locked the unit and drove home without stopping to eat.

She set the parcel on the kitchen counter and the box on the kitchen table, made tea, and lifted the lid the way she opened a brief, reading the spine of the top folder first, because the spine carried the file's register before the file did.

The spine was in her father's hand. Vryonis v. Argyros, NSW Supreme Court probate, judgment 1981, junior counsel of record Y. Argyros, BMA file 04/81. Returned to private custody on cessation of retainer, 17 December 1981. Do not destroy.

The folder was the standard buff cardboard a Sydney solicitor of his generation carried a private matter in, with a single small yellow adhesive flag on the lower edge, the same brand as the flags in the Halsbury's at the unit and the same brand she had been ordering for her own files since 2014. She had ordered it because he had ordered it. She had never told herself that.

It was thick, four hundred pages or more, organized in the sub-folder structure he had kept in practice and her own assistant kept at the firm, because he had taught it to a senior associate in 2014 in the same session at which he handed his practising certificate back. Pleadings, affidavits, exhibits, case authorities, counsel notes, junior counsel correspondence, client correspondence, chambers memoranda, judgment.
She opened the exhibits first. He had trained her to, because the exhibits were load-bearing and the judgment was only the court's reading of them.
The lead exhibit was a 1907 Greek shipping registry extract.

It was not the extract Holloway had sent her on Monday. It was an extract of the same period, from the same Lloyd's-trained clerk in Singapore, for the same Dampier Peninsula run, naming four of the same masters. It carried four vessel names. Two of them were identical to two of the four she had written on the back of a Coles receipt at six twenty that morning.
She read the two names a second time and a third, which she did not need to do, and the rereading was the only cost she let herself spend on the page.

The next exhibit was a foolscap sheet in his hand, titled in pencil Argyros-line 1907 vessel-naming convention, draft note for chambers consultation, do not file. Two pages. He had set out the four vessels' first letters in registry order, the same four letters she had been copying onto receipts and notepads since Tuesday. He had not written the gloss. Above the letters he had written counsel assumption, and below them pending verification, with one short horizontal line drawn under it, the kind of line Eleni drew under a note she had no evidentiary basis to commit to yet.
She did not write the gloss either.

Next came a sheaf of seven Lloyd's listings, cross-checked in his hand against the four vessels and against four others of the period out of Pothia and Symi. These were not the passes she had run on Tuesday. These were the cross-checks of a more senior solicitor: the transshipment dates set against the State Library of Western Australia's pearling-season calendar, against the Darwin port officer's stamp dates, against the Pothia harbour master's departure manifests, in the annotated hand of a man who had spent six months on the exhibit and had not been allowed to put any of it before a court.

Then a single page. Junior counsel research note. Ronald Pavlou consulted informally re probate-as-vehicle question. Three lines named Pavlou as a Macquarie Street barrister her father had met for coffee at the Wentworth at the end of October 1981, to ask whether a court could be invited to treat the registry's over-ordering as load-bearing exhibit material under the rules of evidence as they then stood. Pavlou's answer was recorded in two words. Not possible. Under them, in pencil, a fourth line. No further route through this channel.
She set the page beside the listings and kept reading.

She read the exhibits for four hours while the afternoon got into the kitchen, his marginal annotations at every entry. They were the annotations of a man who had taken the file as far as a junior counsel of record in 1981 could take a file whose load-bearing exhibit he was not permitted to name in open court. They were precise. They did not romanticize.

At half past three she came to counsel notes. The first item was a hand-bound stitched booklet of about thirty pages, his closing-argument draft, an Argyros-line defence to a Vryonis-line probate claim, the load-bearing exhibit footnoted at every turn, the argument running carefully around the absence of the network as a term the court had no vocabulary for. The flag on the cover said not delivered.

She had read everything but the judgment by twenty to six. The judgment sat at the back of the folder where the file ended, and he had trained her to read it last, because it was the institutional reading and the institutional reading was the last document the lawyer read.
She put the folder back in the box and set the lid on top, and did not tape it.

On the back of the parcel on the counter, in pencil, in his hand, was a single line. From your grandfather Kostas, Kingsford kitchen 1998, returned to me 2004. K. died 12 October 2004. It was tied in the knot her father tied, the four-loop carrick bend she had watched him make since she was six. She did not untie it.
She sat down at the table with the box and the parcel and the four initials on the receipt in her wallet in the bag by the door, and she did not call anyone.

There were people she could have called. Aspasia, who had marked the saint's days on the Pothia calendar for forty years and would have known in one sentence who Manolis Argyros had been. The cousin in Earlwood. Her assistant, even, who could have pulled the 1981 cause papers on Monday without being told why. She held the phone long enough to register that she was holding it, and set it face down, because a call was a thing you could not unmake, and she did not yet know what she would be asking for, or whom it would cost.

She did not name the cost. She had been trained out of naming it by the man who had built the file at her elbow, who had written constrained by considerations not on the face of the file in a chambers memorandum she had read an hour before, and whose discipline of not-writing she had practised at her own desk on Macquarie Street since 2014 without once telling herself it had been his first.
At twenty past seven she turned the kitchen light on, rinsed the cold cup, and went to bed.

She thought about her father as the man who had handed his certificate back at sixty-one because, he told her mother at the Kingsford table, he had been carrying the case thirty-three years and was tired. She had not asked him about the case. The not-asking had become a folder on a table on the other side of the bedroom wall, and now there was no one left to ask, and the only voice the file would answer in was her own reading of it.

There were two things in it she had not yet done. She had not read the judgment, and the judgment could keep; she was not ready to let the court read for her tonight. And she had not run her fingers along the back wall of the interior pocket, the way he had trained her to clear a pocket before she called a folder closed, because she had spent the afternoon reading him and not thinking like him.
